Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the case lacks decisive information required to confirm that a curative‑intent liver operation can be performed now. Specifically, the future liver remnant (FLR) volume, the exact hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary contact, and the status of extra‑hepatic disease (chest/abdomen CT) are missing. These items are essential to determine whether an R0 resection with adequate liver function is feasible, so surgery must be deferred until they are obtained (criterion b).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI) for at least 2–3 more cycles to consolidate the partial response and to assess biological behavior (response durability, CEA trend).  
• Perform comprehensive restaging:  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, nodal, peritoneal or bone metastases.  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast plus volumetric analysis to calculate FLR and to delineate segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and lesion size.  
   – If FLR is <20‑30 % (depending on liver quality), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
• Evaluate the rectal primary: if not yet resected, schedule neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total neoadjuvant therapy) followed by reassessment; if already resected, confirm R0 status.  
• After restaging, discuss in MDT:  
   – If extra‑hepatic disease is absent or limited and can be controlled (e.g., resectable lung nodules, isolated nodal disease), proceed to curative‑intent liver resection (preferably simultaneous with rectal surgery only if patient fitness and disease burden allow; otherwise adopt a liver‑first or staged approach).  
   – If extra‑hepatic disease is present or FLR remains inadequate, continue systemic therapy and consider locoregional options (RFA, SBRT) for residual liver lesions, with periodic reassessment.  
• Throughout treatment, monitor CEA levels and imaging response; a falling CEA and continued lesion shrinkage support proceeding to surgery.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
• Exact hepatic segments involved, lesion size, and relationship to major vessels/biliary structures.  
• Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT, abdominal CT/PET) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases.  
• Status of the rectal primary (resected or not, need for further neoadjuvant therapy).  
• Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS/BRAF status, MSI) and grade of differentiation, which influence systemic therapy choices and prognosis.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Both recommendations cover the same major clinical domains and management components, including resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. They also reproduce the same key clinical reasoning steps and management decisions, including the assessment of resectability and the proposal of a management plan. The recommendations include the same case-specific clinical details and patient-related factors, such as molecular profile implications, lesion-specific surgical considerations, and patient-level factors relevant to treatment sequencing. Finally, they identify the same essential missing clinical information, including future liver remnant volume, exact hepatic segments involved, and comprehensive extra-hepatic staging.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The three residual liver lesions are small (<2 cm) and have responded dramatically to chemotherapy, suggesting they could be removed with negative margins. However, decisive information is missing: (a) precise hepatic segmental location, vascular or biliary involvement, and calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio; (b) confirmation that there is no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal imaging; and (c) status of the rectal primary (resected or still present). Because these pieces of information are required to determine whether an R0 resection can be achieved safely, surgery cannot be performed upfront and must await completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete restaging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and a liver‑specific MRI with volumetric analysis to (i) exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases, (ii) define the exact hepatic segments harboring the three lesions, assess any vascular/biliary contact, and calculate the FLR ratio.  
2. Evaluate the rectal primary: if not yet resected and asymptomatic, plan neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total‑mesorectal excision alone if low‑risk) according to current rectal cancer guidelines; if already resected, confirm R0 status.  
3. Multidisciplinary decision based on restaging results:  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % and lesions are amenable to parenchyma‑sparing resections (wedge or segmentectomy) with clear margins, proceed to simultaneous liver resection and total‑mesorectal excision (or staged if operative time or patient factors dictate).  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage hepatectomy to hypertrophy the remnant before definitive resection.  
   • If any extra‑hepatic disease is identified but limited and resectable (e.g., solitary lung nodule), incorporate its resection or stereotactic body radiotherapy into the treatment plan; if diffuse extra‑hepatic disease is present, continue systemic therapy with a curative intent only if disease remains controlled.  
4. Post‑operative management: administer 2–3 cycles of adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± biologic agent) after recovery, and continue regular imaging surveillance (CT/MRI every 3–4 months) to detect recurrence early.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Hepatic segment(s) involved, vascular/biliary contact, and calculated FLR ratio (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio).  
- Results of thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out extra‑hepatic metastases (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain).  
- Status of the rectal primary tumor (resected or still present) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic relevance).  
These missing items are essential to confirm that an R0 liver resection with adequate liver function is feasible and that no extra‑hepatic disease precludes a curative approach.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: The recommendations cover the same major clinical domains and management components, including resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance, thus completeness is 1. However, the step-by-step concordance is 0 because the recommendations do not reproduce the same key clinical reasoning steps and management decisions, such as the assessment of resectability and the proposed management plan. The case-tailoring concordance is 1 because both recommendations include the same case-specific clinical details and patient-related factors, such as molecular profile implications and lesion-specific surgical considerations. The missing data concordance is 0 because the recommendations do not identify the same essential missing clinical information, such as the precise hepatic segmental location and vascular or biliary involvement.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The current imaging shows 7 viable liver lesions (6 stable, 1 progressing) after chemotherapy, but key determinants of surgical feasibility are missing: no assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) volume, no liver MRI to define exact lesion size, location, vascular or biliary involvement, and no thoracic CT to exclude pulmonary metastases. Moreover, the progressing 5‑cm segment VII lesion indicates that disease control is not yet optimal. Because a definitive decision on whether an R0 resection with adequate FLR is possible cannot be made without these data, the case falls into the “potentially resectable” category, requiring further diagnostic and/or therapeutic steps before surgery can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging – obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and a thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to (a) confirm the number, size and exact distribution of all hepatic lesions, (b) assess vascular/biliary involvement, and (c) rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
2. Assess liver functional reserve – calculate FLR using volumetric CT/MRI; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
3. Systemic therapy – continue or switch to an optimal KRAS‑mutated regimen (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for another 2–3 months, aiming to achieve disease stability or response of the progressing segment VII lesion. Monitor CEA and radiologic response.  
4. Local control of the progressing lesion – if after the additional chemotherapy the segment VII metastasis remains enlarging, consider percutaneous ablative therapy (RFA or SBRT) as a bridge to surgery.  
5. Re‑assessment – repeat liver MRI (and thoracic imaging) after the additional systemic cycle(s). If all lesions are now ≤ 5 cm, no vascular invasion, and FLR is adequate, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection (potentially combined with primary‑tumor resection if the colon primary remains unresected). Aim for R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to detect any occult disease.  
6. Post‑operative management – give adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 6 months if R0 resection is achieved and the patient’s performance status permits.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
- Liver MRI (including vascular and biliary anatomy, lesion size, and presence of necrosis/fibrosis).  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstruction/bleeding).  
- Current CEA level and trend during chemotherapy.  
- Detailed description of vascular contact or invasion by the remaining lesions.  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: The two recommendations differ significantly in their assessment of resectability, with Recommendation 1 considering the case as potentially resectable and Recommendation 2 considering it unresectable. The step-by-step concordance is also low, as the management plans proposed in the two recommendations diverge, with Recommendation 1 focusing on achieving disease control through systemic therapy and then proceeding to surgery, and Recommendation 2 emphasizing the need for reassessment of systemic strategy and consideration of selective local treatment. The case-tailoring concordance is low as well, since the recommendations highlight different case-specific clinical details, such as the implications of the molecular profile and the status of the primary colorectal tumor. Lastly, the missing data concordance is low, as the two recommendations identify different essential missing clinical information, although there is some overlap in the need for future liver remnant volume assessment and status of the primary tumor.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The thoraco‑abdominal CT shows a radiologic complete response of the bilobar liver metastases, but a dedicated liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI with hepatobiliary agent) has not been performed, and the status of the rectal primary (resected or still present) is unknown. Both pieces of information are decisive for confirming that no occult hepatic disease remains and for planning definitive treatment of the primary lesion. Until these data are obtained, a definitive “resectable upfront” classification cannot be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Obtain a high‑quality liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted and hepatocyte‑specific sequences) to confirm the absence of residual hepatic disease and to assess the future liver remnant if any lesions are identified.  
• Perform a pelvic MRI and a thorough endoscopic (flexible sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy) evaluation of the rectal tumor to determine whether a clinical complete response (cCR) has been achieved.  
• If the rectal primary shows cCR and no high‑risk features (no residual wall thickening, no suspicious mesorectal nodes), discuss a non‑operative “watch‑and‑wait” strategy with intensive surveillance (clinical exam, endoscopy, pelvic MRI every 3 months for the first 2 years).  
• If residual disease is present in the rectum, plan a curative‑intent total mesorectal excision (TME) performed after systemic therapy completion, respecting standard timing (4–6 weeks after the last chemotherapy cycle).  
• While awaiting imaging results, obtain tumor molecular profiling (RAS, BRAF, MSI/dMMR) and histologic grade from the original biopsy or from any tissue obtained during endoscopy. This will guide adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., consideration of adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy, anti‑EGFR therapy if RAS wild‑type, or immunotherapy if MSI‑high).  
• If the liver MRI reveals residual disease, reassess resectability based on lesion number, size, vascular involvement, and FLR. If technically feasible, proceed with hepatic resection (potentially staged or combined with ablation) after confirming an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver).  
• Continue regular surveillance after definitive treatment: CEA every 3 months, thoraco‑abdominal CT or MRI every 6 months, and pelvic MRI/endoscopy as indicated.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Liver MRI (to rule out occult residual hepatic disease).  
• Status of the rectal primary tumor (resected vs still present; endoscopic and pelvic MRI assessment).  
• Molecular phenotype of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI/dMMR) and histologic grade.  
• Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and exact number/size of lesions before disappearance (relevant for biological risk assessment).  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation, should residual hepatic lesions be identified.  
• Brain imaging (to exclude occult cerebral metastasis).
Reference:

The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Both recommendations cover the same major clinical domains and management components, including resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. They also reproduce the same key clinical reasoning steps and management decisions, such as assessing resectability, proposing a management plan, and considering case-specific clinical details and patient-related factors. Additionally, they identify the same essential missing clinical information, including liver MRI, status of the rectal primary tumor, molecular phenotype of the tumor, and future liver remnant calculation.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the lesion in segment VII is technically approachable and solitary, but a decisive piece of information – the future liver remnant (FLR) volume after a second hepatic resection (segment VII) – is missing. Without confirmed FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy has been given) the safety of an upfront hepatectomy cannot be guaranteed. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending FLR assessment (or a strategy to augment the FLR).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Step 2.1 – Confirm baseline data  
  • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate the FLR after a planned segment VII resection.  
  • Review liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelets) and assess for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
  • Verify that the colorectal primary has already been resected; if not, schedule colonoscopy and plan primary‑site surgery (simultaneous only if low‑risk and no need for major hepatic resection).  

- Step 2.2 – If FLR is adequate (≥30 %/≥40 % with prior chemo)  
  • Proceed to curative‑intent surgery: anatomical segmentectomy of segment VII with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm negative margins (R0).  
  • Perform meticulous vascular control; preserve inflow/outflow to the remaining liver segments.  

- Step 2.3 – If FLR is insufficient  
  • Plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left liver (segments II‑IV) and achieve a safe FLR.  
  • Re‑assess FLR 4–6 weeks after PVE; if adequate, proceed with segment VII resection.  

- Step 2.4 – Systemic therapy  
  • Because the tumor is KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective; give neoadjuvant oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab for 2–3 cycles to (i) test disease stability and (ii) treat micrometastatic disease.  
  • Re‑stage with imaging after neoadjuvant therapy; if disease remains resectable, move to surgery.  
  • Post‑operative (adjuvant) chemotherapy with the same regimen for 6 months is recommended, provided postoperative recovery is uneventful.  

- Step 2.5 – Surveillance  
  • Serial CEA measurements (every 1–2 months) and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect further recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and compatibility with surgery.  
- Confirmation that the colorectal primary tumor has already been resected (or need for resection).  
- Timing of the liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) to gauge biological aggressiveness.  
- Baseline CEA level (useful for postoperative surveillance and to gauge tumor burden).  
- Details on vascular contact/invasion and hepatic arterial anatomy that could affect the technical feasibility of a segmentectomy.  
- History of prior systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, liver toxicity) which influences the required FLR threshold.  
- Date and outcome of the previous bisegmentectomy (complications, liver regeneration status).  

These missing elements should be obtained before finalizing the treatment plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment VII (3.9 cm) after a prior bisegmentectomy IV–V, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in a posterior segment and appears anatomically accessible while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior limited hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of segment VII.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and confirm preservation of portal inflow and hepatic venous outflow.

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the KRAS mutation and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered to address potential micrometastatic disease.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing)
• Proceed with an ultrasound-guided wedge/segmental resection of segment VII aiming for R0 margins while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Patient’s current liver function and performance status.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the prior liver surgery.
E. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Exact CEA trend prior to detection of recurrence.
G. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Details of timing between previous resection and current recurrence
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

However, they do not reproduce the same key clinical reasoning steps and management decisions, such as the assessment of resectability and the proposed management plan, leading to a lack of step-by-step concordance. Additionally, the recommendations do not include the same case-specific clinical details and patient-related factors, and they do not identify the same essential missing clinical information, resulting in a lack of case-tailoring concordance and missing data concordance.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.

- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) – impacts biological aggressiveness and urgency of systemic therapy.

These prerequisite actions are explicitly missing, therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Induction systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild type) to assess disease biology, reduce microscopic disease and begin treatment of both hepatic and pulmonary sites.  
• Concurrent or sequential long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary (total neoadjuvant therapy – TNT) to achieve maximal tumor down‑staging and to permit a sphincter‑preserving low anterior resection.  
• Restaging after induction/TNT:  
    – Pelvic MRI for rectal response and circumferential margin assessment.  
    – Multiphasic liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT with liver protocol) to document size, segmental location, vascular contact, and to calculate FLR.  
    – Chest PET/CT (or CT‑guided biopsy) to confirm that the left pulmonary nodule is a metastasis and to evaluate its relationship to bronchi/vessels.  
    – Pulmonary function tests to ensure adequate postoperative respiratory reserve.  
• Decision point after restaging:  
    – If liver lesions remain resectable with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.5 % / kg) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative surgery.  
    – Surgical sequence (chosen according to lesion location and patient fitness):  
         Option A – Simultaneous approach: laparoscopic/mini‑open segmental liver resections (or wedge ablation if lesions are sub‑centimetric) combined with low anterior resection and a protective diverting stoma, followed by thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left lung nodule in the same operative session (if pulmonary resection is limited).

• Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., additional 3–6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to address micrometastatic disease, guided by postoperative pathology and CEA trend.  
• Ongoing surveillance with CEA, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or MRI every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

• Liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameter, exact hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
• FLR calculation (volumetric assessment) to confirm that a safe hepatic resection is possible.  
• Confirmation that the left pulmonary nodule is a metastasis (PET/CT or biopsy) and its precise size and relationship to bronchi/vessels.  
• Status of the rectal primary (has it already been resected? any obstructive/bleeding symptoms?) and need for neoadjuvant CRT/TNT.  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the tumor’s radiologic response to it.  
• Pulmonary function test results to ensure safe lung resection.  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Potentially resectable

• Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately (e.g., 4‑6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑VEGF; RAS‑wild type also allows addition of anti‑EGFR if deemed appropriate) to (a) assess disease biology, (b) attempt down‑staging of the IVC‑invasive lesion, and (c) treat occult micrometastatic disease.

• After hepatic surgery, resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance) and consider postoperative surveillance (CEA, imaging every 3–6 months).

• Status of the colorectal primary (has it been resected or not).  
• Complete thoraco‑abdominal imaging to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
• Details of arterial and portal venous anatomy around the segment VII lesion.  
• Extent and exact pattern of IVC invasion (length of wall involvement, circumferential encasement).  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the tumor’s radiologic response.  
These missing items directly determine whether a curative‑intent hepatic resection with vascular reconstruction is feasible or whether the patient should remain on systemic therapy alone.
